In order to summarize everything discussed so far into a single concept, it is first necessary to remind the reader: that the concern here is not the origin of experience, but rather what lies within it. The former belongs to empirical psychology, and even there it could never be properly developed without the latter, which belongs to the critique of cognition and especially of the understanding.

Experience consists of <term>Anschauungen</term> <gloss>intuitions or sensory perceptions</gloss>, which belong to sensibility, and of judgments, which are solely the business of the understanding. However, those judgments that the understanding forms solely from sensory intuitions are still far from being judgments of experience. For in the former case, the judgment would only connect perceptions as they are given in sensory intuition; in the latter case, however, the judgments are intended to express what experience in general contains, and thus not what is contained in mere perception, whose validity is merely subjective. The judgment of experience must therefore add something to the sensory intuition and its logical connection (after it has been made general through comparison) in a judgment; this addition determines the synthetic judgment as necessary and thereby as universally valid. This can be nothing other than that concept which represents the intuition as determined in itself in respect to one form of judgment rather than another.

<summary>Kant distinguishes between the psychological origin of experience and the structural components of cognition. He explains that judgments of experience require a specific conceptual addition to mere sensory perception to achieve universal validity.</summary>
<keywords>experience, empirical psychology, understanding, intuition, judgment of experience, sensibility, synthetic judgment, universal validity</keywords>

### *On the proportionality of the limbs.* Chap. CLXXV.

All the parts of any animal must be corresponding to its whole: that is, a creature that is short and thick must have every limb within itself short and thick, and one that is long and slender should have long and slender limbs, and the average one should have limbs of the same average quality. The joint of the arm with its hand diminishes when clenching and thickens when the hand is opened. The arm between the elbow and the hand does the opposite in all its directions. ### CHAPTER LXVI.

**How the next day we sent messengers to the <term>Caciques</term> <gloss>chiefs</gloss> of Tlascala, entreating them for peace, and what they did regarding this.**

After the battle I described had passed, in which we captured the three principal Indians, our Captain Cortés immediately sent them, along with the two who were in our camp and had gone other times as messengers. He ordered them to tell the <term>Caciques</term> of Tlascala that we begged them to come in peace at once, and to give us passage through their land to go to Mexico <note>Tenochtitlan</note>, as we have sent word to them other times. And if they do not come now, we will kill all their people; and because we like them very much and wish to have them as brothers, we would not want to anger them if they had not given cause for it. Many flattering words were said to them to attract them to our friendship. Those messengers went willingly at once to the capital of Tlascala and delivered their embassy to all the <term>Caciques</term> already named by me, whom they found together with many other elders and <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>. They were very sad, both because of the poor success of the war and because of the death of the captains, relatives, or sons of theirs who died in the battles. It is said they did not want to listen to them willingly; and what they agreed upon regarding this was that they immediately ordered all the diviners and <term>Papas</term> to be called, and others who cast lots, whom they call <term>Tacalnagual</term> <gloss>sorcerers/shape-shifters</gloss>, who are like wizards. They told them to look through their divinations, spells, and lots to see what kind of people we were, and if we could be defeated by giving us war day and night continuously, and also to know if we were <term>Teules</term> <gloss>divine beings/demons</gloss>, just as the people of Cempoal said (whom I have said other times are evil things like demons), and what things we ate, and to look into all this with great diligence. 

<margin>What the diviners and their sorcerers said of our men.</margin>
After the diviners, wizards, and many <term>Papas</term> gathered and performed their divinations and cast their lots and all that they were accustomed to do, it appears they said that in the lots they found that we were men of bone and flesh, and that we ate chickens, dogs, bread, and fruit when we had it, and that we did not eat the flesh of Indians nor the hearts of those we killed. Because, as it appeared, the friendly Indians we brought from Cempoal made them believe we were <term>Teules</term>, and that we ate the hearts of Indians, and that the serpentines <note>light cannons</note> threw lightning bolts like those that fall from the sky, and that the greyhound was a tiger or a lion, and that the horses were for spearing the Indians whenever we wanted to kill them; and they told them many other childish things. 

<margin>The Indian diviners make them believe that we have no strength at night.</margin>
Returning to the <term>Papas</term>, the worst of all that their <term>Papas</term> and diviners told them was that by day we could not be defeated, but only by night, because as it grew dark our strength was taken from us. Furthermore, the sorcerers told them that we were brave and that we had all these virtues by day until the sun set, but as soon as night fell we had no strength at all. When the <term>Caciques</term> heard this and held it as very certain, they sent word of it to their Captain General Xicotenga, so that he might come quickly one night with great powers to give us war. When he learned this, he gathered about ten thousand of the bravest Indians he had and came to our camp. From three sides they began to give us a hand of arrows, and to throw darts with their one-pronged and two-pronged throwing sticks, and those with swords, clubs, and two-handed swords from another side. Once the sick had recovered, and since we had already been there for three days, the women we had sent out arrived. They reported that they had found very few people, and that everyone had gone to the cows <note>the American bison or buffalo</note>, as it was the season for them. We ordered those who had been ill to remain, and those who were well to go with us. We arranged that, after two days' journey from there, those same women would go with two of us to fetch people and bring them to the trail to receive us. With this settled, the next morning all those who were strongest set out with us. After three days' travel we stopped, and the following day Alonso del Castillo set out with Estebanico the black man <note>Estevanico, an enslaved Moroccan and one of the four survivors of the Narváez expedition</note>, taking the two women as guides. The one who was a captive led them to a river that flowed between some mountains where there was a village in which her father lived; these were the first houses we saw that had the appearance and fashion of such <note>referring to permanent, settled dwellings rather than temporary huts</note>.

Castillo and Estebanico arrived back at the place where they had left us, bringing five or six of those Indians. Castillo reported how he had found houses of permanent residence where the people ate beans and squashes, and that he had seen maize <gloss>corn</gloss>. This was the thing in the world that cheered us most, and for it we gave infinite thanks to our Lord. He said that the black man was coming with all the people from the houses to wait on the trail nearby; for this reason we set out. Having walked a league and a half, we met the black man and the people who were coming to receive us; they gave us beans and many squashes to eat and to carry water, and robes made of cowhide <note>bison robes</note>, and other things.

As these people and those who came with us were enemies and did not understand each other, we dismissed the former group, giving them what had been given to us, and we went with the new people. Six leagues from there, as night was falling, we arrived at their houses, where they made great festivities for us. We stayed here one day, and the next we departed, taking them with us to other settled houses where they ate the same as they did. From then on there was a new custom: those who knew of our coming did not come out to receive us on the roads as the others had done; instead, we found them in their houses, and they had built others for us. They were all seated, all of them with their faces turned toward the wall and their heads bowed and their hair pulled over their eyes, and their possessions placed in a heap in the middle of the house. From this point forward they began to give us many robes of skin, and they had nothing they would not give us.

They are the people of the best bodies we saw, and of the greatest liveliness and ability, and those who best understood us and answered what we asked. We called them "those of the Cows" <note>the Jumanos</note>, because the majority of the cows that are killed are near there, and because for more than fifty leagues up that river, they go killing many of them. These people go entirely naked, in the manner of the first ones we found. The women go covered with some deer skins, as do a few men, specifically the old ones who are no longer fit for war. It is a very populated land.

We asked them why they did not sow maize; they answered us that they did so to avoid losing what they sowed, because for two years in a row the rains had failed them, and the weather had been so dry that the moles had destroyed all their maize, and they would not dare to sow again until it had first rained heavily. They begged us to tell the sky to rain and to pray for it, and we promised them to do so. We also wanted to know where they had brought that maize from, and they told us from where the sun set, and that it existed throughout all that land; but that the closest place was by that path.

We asked them which way we should go, and to inform us of the road, because they did not want to go there themselves. They told us that the path was up that river toward the North, and that in seventeen days' journey we would find nothing else to eat but a fruit they call <term>chacan</term>, which they crush between stones; even after this effort it cannot be eaten, being so harsh and dry. And this was the truth, for they showed it to us there and we could not eat it. They also told us that while we went up the river, we would always be traveling through people who were their enemies and spoke their same language, and who had nothing to give us to eat; but they would receive us with very good will and give us many cotton blankets and skins and other things they possessed; but still, it seemed to them that we should by no means take that path.

Doubting what we should do and which path we should take that would best serve our purpose and benefit, we stayed with them for two days. They gave us beans and squashes to eat. Their manner of cooking them is so novel that, because it is so, I wanted to set it down here, so that it may be seen and known how diverse and strange are the wits and industries of human beings. They do not possess pots; to cook what they want, they fill half a large squash with water, and into the fire they throw many stones of the kind that catch heat most easily. When they see the stones are glowing, they take them up with wooden tongs and throw them into that water in the squash until they make it boil with the heat the stones carry. When they see the water boils, they throw in what they are to cook, and during all this time they do nothing but take out some stones and throw in other glowing ones so that the water boils to cook what they want, and thus they cook it.
